claims.text: Conventional casting can produce eutectic high-entropy alloys with a fine dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
Conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloys contain randomly oriented lamellar colonies with a high density of misaligned internal boundaries.
The misaligned internal boundaries promote microcrack initiation during room-temperature deformation.
Directional solidification using a controlled thermal gradient and solidification-front velocity will preferentially align lamellar colonies along the tensile axis.
Aligned lamellar colonies present fewer misoriented interphase boundaries that act as stress concentrators.
Reducing unfavorable boundary orientations will decrease local stress concentrations.
Reducing unfavorable boundary orientations will suppress microcrack nucleation.
Directional solidification can preserve the fine lamellar spacing of the alloy while aligning its colonies.
Fine lamellar spacing contributes to high strength.
Directionally solidified samples will have higher room-temperature yield and ultimate tensile strength than conventionally cast samples of the same composition.
Directionally solidified samples will have greater room-temperature elongation to failure than conventionally cast samples.
Directionally solidified samples will exhibit lower microcrack density than conventionally cast samples.
The simultaneous strength and ductility benefits occur only within an alloy-dependent range of directional-solidification parameters.
Changes in alloy composition or processing conditions outside the effective range may eliminate the predicted improvements.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements is uncertain and depends on optimization of the directional-solidification parameters.
